text.p: Israeli prosecutors have promised a decision by early next week on who, if anyone, to charge in a corruption scandal that first erupted in January over the ill-fated appointment of an attorney general.
Israeli police confirmed on Wednesday they had recommended that charges of fraud and breach of trust be brought against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. But a decision rests with prosecutors.

Because police have yet to make public their recommendations, the Israeli people have had to rely on leaks to the media -- many of them only partial leaks -- about what investigators have discovered over the last 12 weeks.
With so many "ifs" yet to be addressed, it was by no means clear whether the Israeli leader elected last May would be charged or forced to resign.
Netanyahu's lawyer said the police recommendation to indict was itself conditioned on the prime minister's being questioned again.
The police report, based on 60 depositions, ran to 995 pages. The affair emerged last January.

Israel's Channel One television alleged at the time that a Netanyahu ally on trial had pushed political crony Roni Bar-On for the attorney general's job in the hope of winning a plea bargain. Police launched an investigation.

Ever since, suspicions have swirled around Justice Minister Tzachi Hanegbi, the prime minister's director-general Avigdor Lieberman, and the man on trial, Aryeh Deri of the religious Shas party. All denied any wrongdoing.

The initial television report said that Deri had promised his Shas party's support for Netanyahu's deal with the Palestinians to redeploy in the West Bank town of Hebron in return for the Bar-On appointment.
It was unclear whether the police inquiry verified this aspect of the television report.

No one has suggested that Bar-On himself will face charges even though the affair is known in Israel as the "Bar-On affair". Bar-On himself quit hours after being appointed amid criticism he was professionally unfit for the job.

The Israeli criminal code holds that a public servant who commits any fraud or breach of trust affecting the public -- whether or not such fraud or breach of trust would have been an offense if committed against a private person -- is liable to imprisonment for three years.
